recentItems.title: Why politics feels overwhelming—and how to fix it | Tamara Cofman Wittes | TEDxMidAtlantic
recentItems.description:
Around the world, most people say living in a democracy matters to them — and most also say their democracy isn't working. Tamara Cofman Wittes thinks she knows why: we're practicing democracy too fast. Borrowing Kahneman's split between the fast, emotional mind and the slow, reasoning one, she argues that an attention economy built on conflict has pushed us to do all of our democracy in the reactive register. A viral clip is long enough to start a fight but far too short to change a mind — and "democracy fast," she warns, is a gift to leaders like Putin and Xi, who profit when a society stays angry and divided.

The hopeful turn is that the antidote is already in our hands. Drawing on her work with civic movements abroad, Wittes tells the stories of citizens in Malawi and Venezuela who slowed democracy back down to a human pace — ordinary people who, through patient preparation, drew a clear line between a lie and the truth at moments when an election could have tipped into chaos. What they did is more concrete, and more replicable, than it sounds.

The question she leaves with the audience is whether we'll do the unglamorous work democracy actually runs on — practiced every day, not just on election day, and alongside people we disagree with but who still believe it's worth protecting. What would it take to take our own democracy off the fast track? Tamara Cofman Wittes became the fourth president of the National Democratic Institute in 2024. Before joining the Institute, she served as Director of Foreign Assistance in the U.S Department of State.

Previously, she led the Russia sanctions effort for the State Department's sanctions coordination office. Dr. Wittes also served in the State Department from 2009 - 2012 as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs, coordinating U.S. policy on democracy and human rights in the Middle East during the Arab uprisings.

Dr. Wittes spent nearly twenty years as a foreign policy scholar at the Brookings Institution, including as director of its Center for Middle East Policy. Her analysis focused on U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East, political and economic change in the region, and the Arab-Israel conflict.

She is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University, where she has taught courses in international relations, Middle East policy, and security studies. Dr. Wittes was one of the first recipients of the Rabin-Peres Peace Award, established by President Bill Clinton in 1997.

Dr. Wittes has published three books, most recently Foreign Policy Careers for PhDs: A Practical Guide to a World of Possibilities (Georgetown University Press, 2023). She
holds a bachelor’s in Judaic and Near Eastern studies from Oberlin College, and master’s and doctoral degrees in Government from Georgetown University. She is a founder of the Leadership Council for Women in National Security, and served on the board of the National Democratic Institute from 2014 - 2022. She is also a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and Women in International Security.

A native of Michigan, Dr. Wittes lives in Washington, D.C., where she tends a robust pollinator garden. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The Art of Not Knowing | Genevieve Richardson | TEDxGUIS Guangzhou Youth
recentItems.description: In this insightful talk, Genevieve Richardson explores society's pressure to have answers, even when we are uncertain or lack sufficient understanding. She challenges the perception that uncertainty is a weakness, arguing instead that recognising what we do not know is an important part of intellectual curiosity and personal growth. Genevieve encourages us to embrace doubt without falling into apathy, question assumptions, and resist the temptation to confuse confidence with knowledge. Her message reminds us that sometimes the greatest step towards understanding is having the courage to say, "I don't know." Year 13 student at British School of Guangzhou, China This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Is a Hot Dog a Sandwich? | Joy Li | TEDxGUIS Guangzhou Youth
recentItems.description: In this thought-provoking talk, Joy Li uses the seemingly simple question, “Is a hot dog a sandwich?” to explore how we categorise, label, and define things, including ourselves. Drawing on her personal journey of identifying as an introvert and searching for a label that truly represented her, Joy challenges the need to fit into predefined identities. She invites us to move beyond asking, “Which label defines me?” and instead consider, “Why do I need a label at all?” Ultimately, her talk encourages us to embrace self-discovery, challenge limiting definitions, and recognise that who we are is not fixed but full of possibilities. Grade 10 student at Guanghou Foreign Languages School, China. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The Myth of Productivity: Why Sleep Matters | Serena Chen | TEDxGUIS Guangzhou Youth
recentItems.description: In this talk, Serena Chen explores the dangers of procrastination, unhealthy work habits, and sacrificing sleep in the pursuit of academic success. Drawing from her personal experience of staying up late even when there was no homework left, she reflects on the misconception that working longer hours and feeling exhausted are signs of productivity and dedication. She challenges this belief by highlighting how sleep deprivation negatively affects concentration, memory, brain function, and physical health. Serena encourages students to rethink their approach to discipline, embrace effective time management, and recognise that adequate rest is not laziness but an essential part of achieving sustainable success. Student at Shenzhen College of International Education, China This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Paying Attention to Our Planet’s Vital Signs | Paula Bontempi, Ph.D | TEDxCapeMay
recentItems.description: When someone we love has changing vital signs, we don't look away—we pay attention, we show up, we learn, and we take action. Our planet deserves the same kind of care. Join Paula Bontempi as she shares how scientists are like doctors - doing regular check-ups on Earth's vital signs—and why the results demand our presence, not just our concern. Paula Bontempi is a Professor of Oceanography at the University of Rhode Island’s Graduate School of Oceanography and served at NASA Headquarters as acting deputy director of the Earth Science Division and as a physical scientist and program manager in ocean biology and biogeochemistry. She served as NASA Program Scientist for instrument and mission science, including the Sea-Viewing Wide Field-of-View Sensor (SeaWiFS), Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (NPP), and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, Ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission. She holds a Ph.D. in Oceanography from URI-GSO, an M.S. in Oceanography from Texas A&M University, and a B.S. in Biology from Boston College. She was a co-Chair of the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) study on Future Directions for Southern Ocean and Antarctic Nearshore and Coastal Research, and the NASEM Committee for Assessing NASA Science Activation 2.0: Progress, Achievements, and Strategic Recommendations. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Mind The Community Gaps | Allison McEntee | TEDxWilmette
recentItems.description:
Gaps in communities exist. Some gaps are functional, while others are social.
After moving to a new town, Allison McEntee was eager to build her community and discovered that belonging wasn't something you find—it was something you build. Through discovering gaps in her community, she explores the overlooked roles of "Builders": the people who make change, take risks, persevere through criticism, and create the connections that bring communities together. In an era of increasing isolation and division, this talk is a call to stop waiting for someone else to fix what's missing and start building it yourself. In a world powered by data, AI, and endless scrolling, Allison believes human connection still matters most. Nine years ago, she founded the Kenilworth Cookbook Club to bring people together around food and conversation. What began at her kitchen table has grown into the nation’s largest network of Cookbook Clubs — creating spaces where strangers become friends and neighbors build lasting bonds. Alongside building community in real life, Allison has spent more than two decades driving growth in the digital world. A seasoned advertising and revenue leader, she has led brand and sales strategy for companies including Nextdoor, Bustle Digital Group, Walmart Connect, Tasting Table, and Food Network. Across both chapters of her career, one belief guides her: meaningful growth — in business and in life — happens because someone chooses to build it. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Girls against girls | Chloe Anderton | TEDxSaint Ignatius College Geelong Youth
recentItems.description:
Tonight, I will explore why girls are taught to compete with each
other. Through the Barbie movie, I look at how girls learn to compare
themselves through social media, school, expectations and the way
we see other girls. I look at how jealousy, judgement and comparison
can make us feel like another girl’s success makes our own success
smaller. I ask what could happen if we changed the way we think
about competition, supported other girls, and learned to be the girl
we needed. Most importantly, I ask, who taught us that girls are
against girls? Student Saint Ignatius College Geelong This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The AI Ethics Crisis | Robert Castello | TEDxSaint Ignatius College Geelong Youth
recentItems.description:
As our world becomes progressively more modern, many people are
adopting the use of AI and are even integrating it into their personal
and business lives. Although these autonomous features may
appear to be optimal, they are but a facade concealing the truth.
And so, with more and more companies beginning to normalise
such technology, ethics are continuing to be questioned time and
time again and whether we get the answers we deserve now fully
depends on the same empty promises we were fed from the start. Student Saint Ignatius College Geelong This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The Erosion of Ambition | Nuwain De Silva | TEDxSaint Ignatius College Geelong Youth
recentItems.description:
When we were young, we dreamed about our futures with no
worries, but as we grow older, we learn to stop dreaming entirely.
Fear, expectations, and comparison slowly erode the stone of
dreams, and when we grow up, that stone is no more. But what if
the greatest obstacle to success isn’t failure itself, but the fact that
we never tried. Because the greatest tragedy isn’t failing on your
dream, it’s failing to try Student Saint Ignatius College Geelong This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
